papers.title: What Carries Forward? Pretraining Disclosure Across Language Model Releases
papers.summary: The paper audits 41 language‑model releases from 17 families, using 24 pretraining‑related indicators from the 2025 Foundation Model Transparency Index. By comparing 24 adjacent releases in ten families, it tracks how disclosure scores change—finding that scores fell in 11 comparisons, rose in six, and stayed the same in seven, with 38 indicator losses and 28 gains overall. The main result is that later model releases do not consistently preserve earlier pretraining disclosure, and gaps remain in areas such as corpus composition and training compute.

papers.title: The State and Fate of Multilingual, Contextual Evaluation in the NLP World
papers.summary: The paper audits 51 recent multilingual evaluation benchmarks that span 242 datasets and 219 languages, focusing on three pillars: coverage, representativeness, and rigor. It finds that coverage is wide but thin—36 % of languages appear in only one benchmark, many regions are near‑zero, and low‑resource languages are evaluated on only 1–3 task categories versus 14 for high‑resource languages—while representativeness is compromised by 56 % of dataset‑language instances being translations from English and limited culturally grounded content, and rigor is weakened by benchmark contamination and parallel‑corpus overlap. The authors synthesize these findings into concrete recommendations for building evaluation frameworks that are natively constructed, culturally grounded, contamination‑aware, and designed to serve the communities whose languages they claim to evaluate, and provide a dashboard with all metadata.

papers.title: Weakness Localization Is Not Enough: State-Aware Recursive Knowledge Improvement for Large Language Models
papers.summary: The paper introduces Recursive Knowledge Improvement (RKI), a method that treats knowledge enhancement as a sequential, state‑aware intervention process. RKI structures knowledge into graph‑based units, localizes weaknesses, estimates the model’s operational knowledge state from diagnostics and past interventions, selects an appropriate intervention, and then re‑evaluates the model before the next round. On HotpotEval and SafeInternalEval, RKI outperforms existing knowledge‑incorporation methods by 18.41 points on average, and the analysis shows that knowledge states give extra guidance for choosing interventions and can shift even when the same weakness remains.

papers.title: Beyond Update Counts: A Control Map for Evaluating Test-Time Model Updates
papers.summary: The paper introduces the Control Map, an evaluation framework that records the exact updates made to a language model before each answer and separately measures acquisition, retention, locality, and performance in new settings. It shows that update counts alone can miss important differences, proving when counts determine final state and how pre‑answer histories limit score differences. Experiments using ControlMap reveal that at a 760 M‑parameter checkpoint, 24 different update schedules with the same count produce 19.7 %–34.2 % accuracy variation, that learning an edit does not guarantee lasting or contained changes, and that no single editor consistently outperforms others across models, benchmarks, and tests.

papers.title: A Quantitative Approach to Asch Conformity in Frontier Large Language Models
papers.summary: The paper introduces a new way to measure conformity in large language models by repeatedly sampling the same question to build a distribution of answers. It then compares this distribution before and after the model is shown a fabricated consensus, using the probabilistic nature of the model to quantify changes. The experiments confirm that frontier LLMs do conform, and the distribution‑to‑distribution comparison offers additional quantitative insight into when and how strongly they conform.
